title: Ki Teitzei: the stragglers (Deuteronomy 25:17–19)
hook: Amalek attacked the weary at the back of the line

segments.voice: Yesterday, shichecha, the forgotten sheaf left for the poor. Your line was forgotten becomes given. Did you let something lost go as a gift? Today, the last words of Ki Teitzei, and a command to remember. Day five hundred eleven.

Watch a big group on the move and the line starts to stretch. A school trip, a hike, a crowd leaving a stadium. The fast walkers pull ahead. The middle keeps pace. And at the back, a gap opens: the kid with the blister, the grandmother who needs to rest, the dad carrying a toddler on his shoulders. Nobody decides to leave them behind. The line just gets longer. Deuteronomy remembers the day someone noticed that gap and used it.
screen: `A LINE STRETCHES.` → `THE GAP AT THE BACK.` → `SOMEONE USED IT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt; how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were enfeebled in thy rear, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God." The story itself is in Exodus, a battle at a place called Rephidim, soon after the sea. Deuteronomy adds the detail that matters. Amalek didn't attack the army at the front. He went for the back of the line, the enfeebled, the faint, the weary. The ones who couldn't fight and couldn't run. And he feared not God: no line he wouldn't cross. The portion ends with a strange double command. Blot out the memory of Amalek, and, in the same breath: "thou shalt not forget." Erase the name, keep the lesson. The rabbis set this passage to be read on the Sabbath before Purim, called Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath of remembering, because tradition traces Haman, the villain of the Purim story, to Amalek. Some rabbinic authorities hold that the ancient nation of Amalek can no longer be identified, and some teachers read Amalek as a way of acting, preying on the weak, that can show up anywhere, even in us. So the memory has two edges. Remember what was done to the stragglers. And notice who's at the back of your own line, because whoever stands there is the one most easily left behind, and most easily hurt.
screen: `REMEMBER WHAT AMALEK DID.` · `HE SMOTE THE HINDMOST.` · `BLOT OUT, AND DON'T FORGET.` · `WHO'S AT THE BACK OF YOUR LINE?` · then, large: `WATCH THE STRAGGLERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look after whoever is at the back. Settle, and breathe. Picture the lines you're part of. Your family, your team at work, your friend group, your congregation, your class. Who in each one is falling behind? The coworker who's quietly drowning. The cousin no one calls. The friend who stopped showing up. The kid who's slower at reading. Find one. You don't have to fix their life. Just picture walking back down the line to where they are, and keeping pace with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. A portion crowded with commandments, ending with the weary at the back of the line.

Your line: watch the stragglers. A week of trees spared, the nearest town, the mother bird, the railing, wages paid by sunset, the forgotten sheaf, and now the back of the line. Today, reach out to one person who's falling behind. Day five hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Jews read Deuteronomy 25:17–19 aloud on Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath before Purim, and Jewish law treats hearing it read each year as a duty; it is also read at the close of Ki Teitzei in late summer.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient grudge against an enemy tribe.
what it means: remember who preys on the weary at the back of the line, and watch who is at the back of yours.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 17 tells the battle; Deuteronomy adds the hindmost; some rabbinic authorities hold Amalek can't be identified today.

notes: Deuteronomy 25:17–19 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Mishnah Yadayim 4:4 (Sennacherib mixed up the nations) is said of Ammon; its application to Amalek is from later authorities; the script says 'rabbinic teaching holds'. Keeper should review this sensitive passage's framing.
Haman as 'the Agagite' (Esther 3:1) linked to Agag, king of Amalek (1 Samuel 15); tradition, not stated in Esther itself.
Shabbat Zachor reading: Mishnah Megillah 3:4; whether hearing it is a biblical obligation is debated.
